title: The rich man's library
hook: Calvisius Sabinus bought slaves to memorize Homer for him (Letters 27)
carry: nobody can learn it for me

segments.voice: Yesterday: rehearse the end. Your line was ready, calmly. What small piece of unfinished business did you set right? Day four hundred fifty-six.

There's a man in Seneca's Rome named Calvisius Sabinus. He's very rich, he wants badly to seem cultured, and he has a memory so poor that he sometimes forgets the names of famous heroes he's trying to mention. So he comes up with a plan only money could buy. He'll purchase education the way he purchases furniture. In the twenty-seventh letter, Seneca tells the story with a straight face. It's also, a little, about saving an article to read later and never reading it. Today: the rich man's library.
screen: `A RICH MAN WITH A POOR MEMORY.` → `EDUCATION, BOUGHT LIKE FURNITURE.` → `THE ARTICLE SAVED FOR LATER.`

segments.voice: First, the purchase. Sabinus buys enslaved men and has each one learn a poet by heart: one knows Homer, another Hesiod, and nine more, one for each of the Greek lyric poets. Seneca says they cost a fortune, because there weren't any to be had, so they had to be made to order. Second, the dinner parties. Sabinus keeps them at his feet while he entertains, asking them for lines to quote, and still gets the lines wrong halfway through. He has decided, Seneca says, that whatever anyone in his house knows, he knows. Third, the joke. A guest named Satellius Quadratus teases him: you should take up wrestling. Sabinus protests that he can barely stay alive, he's so frail. Don't say that, comes the reply. Look how many healthy slaves you have. The point lands. You can't outsource strength, and you can't outsource understanding. We should also say plainly: these were people, owned and made to perform. Seneca tells it as a joke about Sabinus. We'll look straight at slavery itself in a few days. Fourth, Seneca's line. A sound mind, he says, can't be borrowed or bought. In Latin, bona mens nec commodatur nec emitur. And if it were for sale, he adds, there would be no buyers, while bad sense is bought every day. A shelf of books, a playlist of lectures, a friend who knows: all good. But somebody has to do the learning, and it can only be you.
screen: `SABINUS BUYS A MEMORY.` · `LINES AT DINNER, STILL WRONG.` · `TAKE UP WRESTLING.` · `A SOUND MIND CAN'T BE BOUGHT.` · then, large: `NOBODY CAN LEARN IT FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Pick one short thing you've been meaning to actually know rather than just have: a line from a poem, a verse, a friend's phone number, the name of the tree outside. Say it to yourself slowly, once. Then close your eyes and say it again without looking. Then once more. Notice the moment it moves from the page into you. Rest in that small ownership. The bell holds the time.
The rich man's library. Calvisius Sabinus bought people to remember Homer for him, and proved Seneca's point: a sound mind can't be borrowed or bought. Today's word.
Your line: nobody can learn it for me. Take the thing you just memorized and use it once today, out loud or in your head, without looking it up. Day four hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Some people who study the Stoics memorize a few short lines, so the ideas are at hand when they're needed rather than stored on a shelf.

original.note: Latin, Seneca, Letters 27.8: a sound mind is neither lent nor bought.

trapdoor: what you thought: this is a story about a silly rich man.
what it means: understanding has to be built inside you; nobody can hold it for you.

what a scholar hears: Letters 27.5–8; bona mens is Seneca's recurring term for a sound, well-ordered mind, and Seneca says these enslaved readers cost a fortune because they had to be trained to order.
